newsitem.title: USA: Komag stock dives on earnings warning.
newsitem.headline: Komag stock dives on earnings warning.

text.p: Shares of Komag Inc. nosedived Thursday after the company warned results for the rest of the year would fall dramatically short of expectations due to weak demand for disk drives.

Komag, which makes thin-film media used to store data on computer hard disk drives, fell by $7.81 to $16.75 in early afternoon trading on Nasdaq. The stock was the most actively traded on Nasdaq with over 16.4 million shares changing hands.

Komag said late Wednesday it expects to earn less in its second quarter, ending June 29, than the 33 cents a share it made in its first quarter. Komag said sales would be slightly higher than the $167.2 million in the first quarter.

Analysts had expected the San Jose-based company to earn 45 cents a share in the second quarter, according to First Call. In the comparable year-ago quarter Komag had profits of $42.5 million, or 80 cents a share.

Komag attributed the shortfall to weak demand for large disk drives and lower-than-expected production levels. It said second-quarter gross margins would fall slightly below the 23.5 percent reported for the first quarter.
Orders from Seagate Technology Inc., the biggest disk drive maker in the world and Komag's biggest customer, will be cut in half to about 15 percent of sales compared to the first quarter.
Because of the lower Seagate orders, Komag said it will have excess production capacity, which will cause gross margins and earnings for the third and fourth fiscal quarters to decline.

Hambrecht & Quist analyst Todd Bakar cut his rating on Komag to hold from buy and slashed his earnings estimates. He cut his fiscal 1997 estimate to 90 cents a share on $670 million in revenues from $2.20 a share on $783 million in revenues. He also cut fiscal 1998 estimates to $1.60 a share on $790 million in revenues from $3.25 a share on $960 million in revenues.
Glenn Hanus, an analyst at Needham & Co., also cut his estimate to hold from buy and said he expects the stock will trade in the range of $15 to $19 until there are some positive developments.
"The major issue for them is filling the capacity they have put in place that Seagate seems not to need at the moment," Hanus said.
"I think the company's approach was to get the bad news out there and the (projections) they made were probably the pessimistic case," he said.

Komag recently picked up two new customers, International Business Machines Corp. and Maxtor Corp., which will fill some of the gap left by the Seagate shortfall. Those two customers are expected to account for about 10 percent of business in the second quarter and continue to grow, but not enough to fill the entire Seagate shortfall.
Hanus said Komag was affected more than other suppliers to Seagate, which warned of weak earnings earlier this month, because it has a broader customer base than some other Seagate suppliers.

"Other suppliers had made bigger commitments to Seagate and Seagate didn't want to be a gorrilla putting people out of business," Hanus said. "Komag has a more diversified customer base and is able to withstand a cutback better than some other companies that are not as diversified."
